input.ground_truth: Well, this is a problem that can only really be solved by experiment! Especially since we have no idea about a lot of the factors involved (the exact geometry of the rooms, the exact optical properties of the paint/wallpaper, etc etc). The simplest way to measure I can think of would be to use my DSLR with a set exposure time and just take pictures of my desk with the door open and then closed, since that's a fairly objective way to measure how bright it is. If you don't have a DSLR, have fun, come up with your own experiment. Isolate what you're trying to measure as best you can and have at it!

Question: Light Reflection : To maximize bedroom light, do I turn the bathroom light on or close the bathroom door? [w/ Diagram]

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a bedroom and next to it is a bathroom. The bathroom has a light bulb. You want your bedroom to be as bright as possible.

If you **turn on the bathroom light**, the light can shine into the bedroom if the door is open. Light likes to spread out and go into different rooms if there’s nothing blocking it.

But if you **close the bathroom door**, the light from the bathroom can’t get into the bedroom anymore. The door blocks the light.

So, if you want your bedroom to be brighter, you should **leave the bathroom door open and turn on the bathroom light**. That way, more light can come into your bedroom!

But if you close the door, the bathroom light can’t help make your bedroom brighter.

Here’s a simple drawing to help:

```
[Bedroom] <---- [Door Open] ----> [Bathroom] (Light On)
```

Light goes through the open door into the bedroom.

But if the door is closed:

```
[Bedroom] || [Door Closed] || [Bathroom] (Light On)
```

Light stays in the bathroom.

So, to get more light in your bedroom, **open the door and turn on the bathroom light!**
